questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating an Integral Given Another Integral With Reversed Limits of Integration
questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(f(x)-5)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x-5{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =1-5\cdot x\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =1-5(2-0) \\  & =1-5\cdot 2 \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=5$ and ${\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}$ then what is ${\int }_{0}^{6}(3f(x)+3)\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5+\frac{1}{3}={\int }_{0}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{16}{3}={\int }_{0}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{6}(3f(x)+3)\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{0}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{0}^{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3(\frac{16}{3})+3\cdot x\,{|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =16+3(6-0) \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{3}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=8$ and ${\int }_{4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x=4,$ then what is ${\int }_{3}^{6}(5-2f(x))\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8+4 & ={\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 12 & ={\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{6}(5-2f(x))\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{3}^{6}\text{d}x-2{\int }_{3}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot x\,{|}_{3}^{6}-2\cdot 12 \\  & =5(6-3)-24 \\  & =5(3)-24 \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2+6={\int }_{3}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 8={\int }_{3}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{7}(2f(x)+3)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{3}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{3}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2(8)+3\cdot x\,{|}_{3}^{7} \\  & =16+3(7-3) \\  & =28.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Suppose that $f(x)$ is a  function such that ${\int }_{2}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x=8$ and ${\int }_{2}^{0}2f(x)\,\text{d}x=4.$ What is the value of ${\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{0}2f(x)\,\text{d}x & =4 \\ 2{\int }_{2}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =4 \\ -2{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =4 \\ {\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(-2)+8 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $f$ and $g$ be continuous functions such that ${\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x=18,{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{1}{2}g(x)\,\text{d}x=5,$ and ${\int }_{3}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x=4.$ What is the value of ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{1}{2}\,g(x)\,\text{d}x & =5 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =5 \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the adjacent intervals rule and substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the sum rule for definite integrals and substituting the known values, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ 18-10 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ 4 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x=4.$

questions.problem: Suppose that $f(x)$ is a  function such that ${\int }_{5}^{12}f(x)\,\text{d}x=12$ and ${\int }_{5}^{-5}6\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=18.$ What is the value of ${\int }_{-5}^{12}f(x)\,\text{d}x?$

Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{5}^{-5}6\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =18 \\ 6{\int }_{5}^{-5}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =18 \\ -6{\int }_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =18 \\ {\int }_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5}^{12}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{5}^{12}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3+12 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that ${\displaystyle \int_{0}^{6} \, f(x) \; \textrm d x = -54 },$ what is the value of
${\displaystyle \int_{6}^{0} \bigg( \dfrac 1 3 f(x) + 1 \bigg) \; \textrm d x }?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{0}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{6}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=54\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{0}(\frac{1}{3}f(x)+1)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{6}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{6}^{0}1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 54+x\,{|}_{6}^{0} \\  & =18+(0-6) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: If $\displaystyle \int_7^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x = 18$ and $\displaystyle \int_0^{7}f(x)\,\textrm d x = -6$ then what is $\displaystyle \int_0^{10} \big( 2f(x)+1 \big) \,\textrm d x?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\int_0^{7}f(x)\,\textrm d x + \displaystyle \int_7^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x = \displaystyle \int_0^{10}f(x)\,\textrm d x.
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6+18={\int }_{0}^{10}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ 12={\int }_{0}^{10}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{10}(2f(x)+1)\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{10}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{10}\text{d}x \\  & =2(12)+x\,{|}_{0}^{10} \\  & =24+(10-0) \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is a  function such that ${\displaystyle \int_4^1 2 \, f(x) \, \textrm dx = -1}$ 
and ${\displaystyle \int_{1}^{-1} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 2}.$  What is the value of ${\displaystyle \int_{-1}^4 f(x) \, \textrm dx}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the first given integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{1}2\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ 2{\int }_{4}^{1}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ -2{\int }_{1}^{4}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{4}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The second integral can be rewritten as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ -{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
